speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: ...renewing the Superfund bill, and we ran across this cluster of people who were just self-reporting the deaths of children in the neighborhood and cancers, and that their own child had a birth defect, and gee, they wondered if something wasn't wrong, and so we began to organize that neighborhood, and this was in the summer of '84. And the state at the time claimed that they had no knowledge of any possible problem, it was a two and a half times elevated childhood cancer rate compared to national norms, and we saw the progression where the state initially at the point when there was no identified source of the problem, it was just a cancer cluster, and we were investigating, looking at, gee, is this radon gas, could it be, you know, any number of possible things, before we knew what the source of the problem was, the state admitted that there was a high childhood cancer rate in the area, but they couldn't from their preliminary work link it to any environmental hazards, and they just... case closed. When we got involved, we found it interesting that they had not tested the drinking water for the community, but they had tested the groundwater in the area, and they had tested the radiation levels around, and without having tested the drinking water, they said there's no problem here, and so four months of organizing, and in the midst of that, Martin Marietta began to counter organize the neighborhood, and we thought that was interesting. So perhaps it was drinking water, and perhaps it was Martin, but we didn't know all of the mechanisms that had come together to make that make that a reality. But what's of major interest politically is that state health department was very overt in trying to shut this thing up, as was the EPA, and the EPA at the time was trying to prevent the citizens from doing their own health survey, and then when it was clear they were going to do their own health survey, the EPA played the role to make, to convince the leadership of the community group that it would, should, should be the weakest possible survey, very brief, not very in-depth. I was trying to encourage them to do a more elaborate health survey, so it would really provide more information, and so the EPA was trying to prevent, you know, kind of a full exploration of the situation. The EPA was also claiming they didn't know what was the problem.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: How did the EPA do that?

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, their public relations department spent a lot of time... No, CC Forjay was her name, she's no longer around, from what I can tell. But they had a pretty elaborate PR effort, you know, again, this is under the Reagan administration, to rather than serve as a public relations arm to the community, they were actually playing the role of dividing the community leaders from one another and preventing them from doing the fullest level of investigation with their own resources, and I thought that was interesting. And the state health department was refusing to conduct a door-to-door study, and worse than that, they were actually, what's the word I want to use, not threatening people, but they were being very abusive about... in their denials of and acceptance of the information. Like when we went in to meet with the State Health Department, we said "we've gathered all this data from our door-to-door canvas, and we'd like to present it to you, because we feel that you'll find this of interest, and will want to do a more elaborate investigative study of the area," and they would refuse to take the data of the deaths and illnesses that we had documented in the community, claiming it was unscientific, and they didn't want to look at it. We said, "well, of course, it's unscientific, but on the other hand, these are people's individual reports of their own family's deaths and illnesses, and you know, shouldn't you want to corroborate these and do an independent search of the records?" And they didn't, they would not even take the data, and we thought that was odd, and there were a number of odd things that happened. We started searching the records for the water distribution to the community from the Willowbrook Water and Sanitation District, which was the subcontractor for the community from the Denver Water Board. And after the community, people began to search the records. Three days later, the place was torched, went up in flames, and with it all the records, and was regarded by the Bancroft Fire Department to be a fire of suspected arson, but it was never investigated. And so we began to see a lot of cases of now you see it, now you don't. As we began to get on to the fact that Martin Marietta could have been responsible, the state changed its position from saying, "Yes, you have an elevated childhood cancer rate, but we don't know what we don't see there being an environmental cause." Two months down the road, the state changed its position to, "Well, yes, there is an elevated childhood cancer rate, we don't see there being any cause for it, but we don't have the funds to study it." Then, when we really got more into the evidence that Martin was likely the cause for it, then the state changed its position to say "there is no cancer cluster." So, I mean, they completely eliminated it, although the data was the same at every point, and we thought that was odd. So...

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: ...drinking water, so the actually we had 60 minutes out filming one of these meetings in October of 1984 and at that meeting we said, "Why haven't you investigated Mark Marietta yet? We find that they're on the EPA list as a possible pollution source, and you're required under the law to investigate them, and you haven't done that. Why? You know, why haven't you investigated Martin?" And the EPA guy stood up and started screaming that there was no problem at Martin Marietta, and the state also, and the county health department as well, said "there's no problems at Martin, it's too far away, it couldn't possibly be a problem here." And so then we began to investigate the state records and the EPA records of what they actually had on Martin Marietta, and we're shocked to find that Martin is like allowed to dump into Brush Creek, which we found in subsequent investigations pours right into the municipal water supply immediately downhill from the, you know, 5,200 acre aerospace facility. And so, like, with what you're reading about the FBI investigation of the Rocky Flats situation, it's very interesting that now they're saying, as part of the DOE agreement, that they're reclassifying Walnut Creek and Woman Creek, which flow off of the, which are contaminated at some points by Rocky Flats, and then miles away become drinking water for the suburban communities in the Northwest.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, there's really no treatment in any community in the Denver metropolitan area of any for chemical contamination, and at Kassler, which is one of the five sources for the Denver Water Board. We found evidence in the Denver Water Board's own records that pollution was coming down the hill virtually every day, and that they had created a form to track it called the Brush Creek Pollution Sheet, and and it was in files labeled Martin Marietta Pollution, and at the water board, the process for testing the water was five times a day to go down to Brush Creek and smell it and enter the odor, and the inner entries were chemical, chemical, chemical, chemical, chemical, chemical, chemical, for from 63 yeah, 63 you know, up through the 70s and into the 80s, that was the technology for testing the water, and they were delivering it, and so we found this quite shocking. We couldn't quite understand why it would be that the city's water utility would actually support in the poisoning of its own water supplies. It seems unnatural, right? I mean, you would think that the city water agency would stand up and say, "oh my god, our city, you know, our water's being poisoned, we're suing Martin, we have to shut down this facility," and what we found is a pretty elaborate scheme of corruption and collusion between Martin and the Denver Water Board, including exchanges of personnel, and also the similar type of situation between the state and the water board, where you know, which is a pattern that we're seeing as of the present time, where the policymakers in the state health department have actually had direct conflicts of interest with Martin Marietta. The most recent example is the current, well, just just until recently, the head of the water quality control division, which is a branch of the state health department responsible for determining water pollution standards and also for determining permit standards in which companies can get a permit to dump legally into water supplies. We asked for this permit to be revoked from Martin at the point that we discovered that all the parties had evidence it was going straight into a drinking water well, and the state declined to revoke the permit, even given the evidence that we got out of their own files, and declined to revoke the permit, citing that there was, you know, really no evidence that Brush Creek was going into the well, even though we had Denver Water Board documents confirming that it did And worse, the Water Quality Control Division also allowed Martin to escape penalty for violating standards on one of its parameters for the pollutants that it was dumping into Brush Creek and actually waived the state standard because Martin had sent them a letter saying they couldn't afford to treat the water.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: This is like, this this year, so the... That they, that it was going to be expensive for them to do the technologies at the plant that would treat, that would allow them to have the water leave the plant meeting state standards, and so the state water quality control commission just two months ago waived the standard and said "Okay, you can dump at higher levels." Now this is after five years of this whole scandal that we have been publicizing. There are now 16 children that have died in Friendly Hills, and additional other cancers that have occurred. They are literally peppered up and down the street in Friendly Hills, and the Denver Water Board claims that they have sent that water all over the city of Denver. So we believe it's a much bigger scandal than the Friendly Hills situation, and we do see patterns of elevated cancer rates for children in other southwestern metro suburbs, the rates of cancer for children are actually higher than they are in northern Jefferson County, with... that, we would be concerned about with the Rocky Flats effects.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: You're saying, in addition to Friendly Hills downstream from Friendly Hills, there are similar effects, maybe not as strong.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, the water from Kassler was pumped, so it isn't proximity to Martin, except in a general way. Friendly Hills is actually six miles north of Martin, but they pumped it all the way up past the Martin facility and past the Johns Manville area, and then into a community called Chatfield, and then in other suburban areas southwest. They're all in unincorporated Jefferson County. We know they were getting undiluted Kassler water, but they, there are other communities that could have had water diluted from other sources, like Marston or Foothills, that could have gotten diluted quantities of it that we suspect will lead to increased cancer rates overall with a latency period that you would expect from cancer, but the phenomenon in the communities that got the direct water undiluted that we have documented is childhood cancers that have occurred very early after conception, children one years old with brain tumor, that type of, that type of thing, where the cancers doctors have said they believe formed in utero, that the carcinogens were so strong that the effects were in utero for those fetuses, and also a series of birth defects that cluster up and down the street, that if you were pregnant during, you know, a big tidal wave of contamination coming down, we've correlated the worst waves of contamination, and they do seem to associate with patterns of birth defects of the women who gave birth, you know, conceived during those periods, and then gave birth subsequently to children with heart defects and other defects.

speaker: Juc Speaker

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, yes, in Brush Creek itself, in the surface water system, as well as the groundwater system that recharges into it, there is evidence of over 70 contaminants in that system, half of which are known or suspected human carcinogens. So, on any given day, based upon whatever Martin was dumping, we also found, I mean, you think the FBI thing on Rockwell is shocking, there's evidence of 91 different illegal outfall pipes that go straight into Brush Creek. When Martin knew fully well it was going into a municipal water supply at the bottom of the hill.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, yes and no. Now you know we have been very active on this for the last five years. When Lamm was in office, the victims in Friendly Hills asked to meet with Governor Lamm. He didn't, and this was to request a monitoring committee on Martin Marietta, given what we had learned up to that point. And at that point, we didn't know the scale of what we know now, but we knew enough to see that there was a pretty big scandal involved with this, we didn't yet know the state's complicity in it, except in the briefest, most scanty forms, but it was clear that the water board was guilty of criminal activity, as well as Martin Marietta, and also it was clear that the water board and Martin had lied to the public and lied to the EPA about the nature of that situation there, and Governor Lamm invited Martin Marietta personnel into the meeting, who you know that actually lived in the neighborhood, said, "We've never seen any evidence of sick children. These people don't know what they're talking about." And Candy Logue, who had a four-day-old son who died of a cardiac birth defect, ended up, you know, in a big verbal fight with this guy saying, "you should have been there, Mr. Casto, when my son died." We now know that that person in Friendly Hills was being set up by Martin Marietta to counter organize the neighborhood and try to prevent the victims from coming to full discovery about the scale of it. So it was a very ugly situation where the company was actually threatening the residents, and I mean, there was all kinds of nasty things that were going on during that time frame, fortunately, which were not successful. A lot of the people did become so frustrated and despondent and depressed that they dropped out of the effort, but others, you know, who were strong enough, you know, continued on. So that's the kind of gist of the Friendly Hills situation, but in the five years of looking at that, we were so alarmed to find the complicity of the Denver Water Board, and then just really in the last six months or so, we have now seen really extensive documentation of the fact that the state knew it as well, we obtained in the last year evidence of the state health department learning in 1957 that that water supply at Kassler was being polluted by Martin Marietta, which was virtually from the day that Martin opened its doors in 1956. And the state had recommended that there be some sort of alert procedure set up so that when Martin was pouring stuff down the hill, that the cities of Englewood, Aurora, Denver, and Littleton, who were receiving Kassler at that time, could be notified, but we also found documentation that that alert procedure was never put into place or never used.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: Didn't I read somewhere where they built a pretreatment plant to deal with that problem in 1966?

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: No, there was no, no pretreatment. They do have a wastewater facility there, but it's... it doesn't treat the industrial waste.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: The Kassler water treatment people built pretreatment.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: No, no, the treatment at Kassler consisted of filtering the water literally for twigs and leaves. Then they added chlor... they did a chloramination process, which adds disinfectants, and it was delivered. They never had, they never, before 1985 when the water supply was closed down, never tested the water, according to, you know, according to evidence that we've looked at, admit that they never tested the water once for volatile organic chemicals, although they fully knew they were rolling down the hill into their drinking water supply. There's evidence of dead fish, dead beavers, suds on the creek, oil flowing down the surface, and again virtually daily evidence of chemical contamination of Brush Creek, and which would be the case because the EPA and the state had granted Martin a permit to dump on a routine daily basis into that creek, even though we now know they knew it was a drinking water tributary to the well, and on top of that allowed Martin to violate even those levels for a permit they should have never had in the first place allowed it to violate even above those levels several dozen times, and that continues to this day, where they continue to dump into that creek. So, what we found basically is that the state and the EPA allowed Martin Marietta to use a Denver water supply source, basically as a toxic toilet for 30 years of illegal dumping, Martin is one of the only companies in the region that did not take its waste to the Lowry landfill, which you can document by looking at who the list is of the companies that did take waste to Lowry. Martin is not on that list, and with the huge volume of chemicals that Martin was dealing with, it does beg the question, where did the stuff go? We found internal memoranda from the state health department admitting that virtually all of Martin's waste went into the Denver water supply over a 30 year period. Now, Dr. Vernon, who was the head of the health department at that time and who's been in the head of the health department since '77, Dr. Vernon was at the helm when this permit was being reviewed, renewed when the illegal activities were allowed to continue. There is record in the Water Quality Division files of Denver Water Board personnel reporting to the state health department that they had evidence of midnight dumping occurring when Kassler was not staffed, also that they were concerned about pollutants coming into the water supply, and also evidence in the state health department files that there was no follow up to those reports. There's also we also found that a 1973 memo from the Denver Water Board to the EPA and the state indicating that any discharges by Martin into Brush Creek would directly affect the Denver water supplies, and yet the Denver Water Board today, when interviewed as recently as today, claims that there was never any contamination from Brush Creek that affected their drinking water supplies, and they even tried to deny that Brush Creek even formed a part of the Denver water supplies. We found just an unbelievable Chinatown Jack Nicholson type of movie that could be made about the situation between the Denver Water Board and clear evidence of corruption and what we believe to be criminal activity. We've had it reviewed by other criminal investigators who've concluded that yes, certainly in the case of the Denver Water Board, there's clear evidence of criminal activity, destruction of records, and certainly lies to the public and lies to the EPA about the scale of that situation. There, so we have been kind of on the forefront of exposing that situation.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, in 1987 in October of '87 the Friendly Hills people, and myself, and a Denver Police Department detective who lives in Friendly Hills, and whose child is one of the cardiac birth defect cases, we met with Attorney General Woodard and asked him at that time to initiate a criminal investigation of this whole matter, and he indicated that he would do that, that he was very concerned about it, and I've known him for Duane Woodard for 10 years, related to other work that we've done in the state around utility issues and other things, and I've always found him to be very fair and evenhanded and honest. So I felt that I knew him well enough to just ask him directly, you know, "Governor Romer has a big economic development program, is he going to put his finger in this and squelch this investigation? You know, the Denver Water Board is, you know, some of the big Denver Democratic Party muckety mucks that control the Denver Water Board, and are you going to go after them if you find evidence of criminal activities?" "Absolutely, you know, don't you worry about that. I don't care who they are, if we find evidence of that, et cetera, et cetera." So we provided all of our documentation to the state attorney general's office investigators and directed them in other directions as to what we thought were things that we had not yet been able to corroborate, and the investigators were horrified at what we had in our, just in our possession, and what we had in our possession was all from public records, and then so we thought surely something will happen. There were even lower level personnel in charge of Martin at the state health department who had recommended criminal prosecution to the higher ups, but yet Vernon never endorsed that, and so it went on for several months where we knew they were actually collecting records and doing... [unintelligible] Yes, sure does. And we have those documents, we have all those internal memoranda... And so then there was a series of personnel changes that went on. There was a lot of disgruntlement in the Attorney General's office because concurrent with this timeframe the law firm that represents Martin Marietta, Shell at the Arsenal, as well as several other polluters around Superfund site level problems in the state is a law firm, their name is Holm Robertson Owen. You may remember that last year Holme Roberts and Owens put up a candidate to run against Peña for mayor, Don Bain is tied to the law firm that represents the major polluters in the state. Okay, he's a senior partner in that law firm, so we were concerned about that, particularly given the investigation going on at Martin. And anyway, Holme Roberts and Owens, this law firm representing the polluters, went to the state legislature and lobbied the joint budget committee of the legislature to eliminate the funding for the Attorney General's Superfund investigative division.

words: And that was self-supporting, as I recall, they, that money was only there to get the ball rolling, and they could...

words: Recollect it, yes...

speaker: Adrienne Anderson

But it was Holme Roberts and Owens specifically representing their clients that they wanted to eliminate the Attorney General's capacity to investigate them after we had already asked the Attorney General to conduct the investigation on one of their clients, and they were successful in doing that. So, the budget was axed by half for Duane Woodard's Attorney General's office for these kinds of investigations, and Woodard, at that time, I was, we publicly supported him in this. I was impressed that he publicly trashed Holme Roberts and Owens, and said "these people can't beat me in the court, so that's why they're trying to take away my funding, and I'm not going to let this," you know, he stood up to that publicly. So this was going on at the same time. By this point, Romer had been elected, and so we have a change in administration, and Romer had copies of all the correspondence that we were sending to Dr. Vernon about the, you know, the growing numbers of cancers that were being diagnosed out there. Vernon continued to deny that there was any problem in the early stages in '84 when we began to get onto the trail that Martin was a problem. The EPA got involved and did a four month investigation that they spent a quarter of a million dollars on, and then four months hence, and they were going to announce their findings at a public meeting in the Friendly Hills community. There were about 1,100 people, Friendly Hills residents, that came to that meeting, all very worried, you know, the I mean, the people were dropping dead, the children were dropping like flies. And, that community, you know, a very intense, very difficult period. And this was this meeting was December 19th, 1984. And Congressman Schafer led the meeting. The EPA and the state had Vernon, all of the higher ups and the public health agencies were there. Congressman Schafer stood up and said, "Merry Christmas, you have no problem. We can all get home in time for the Bronco game." And then there was a section of people who had actually sat together in the audience that were the Martin Marietta employees that stood up and cheered. And then the victims, you know, who had lost children, you know, had questions. And we had our own expert public health expert flown in from Boston to help analyze the data. And during that meeting, our expert would say, "Excuse me, but I don't see that you've, you know, what's the... you know, the drinking water... you've just..." you know, they put out this little two-page fact sheet that didn't go into any of the data, so we didn't have access to it during the meeting, and no mention was made of Martin Marietta, and the victims who stood up to ask questions were booed by the Martin Marietta personnel in a highly orchestrated little campaign to subvert the residents, and after the meeting, various victims' families who came out of the meeting, then at the front of the door, were then told explicitly by Martin personnel that if they continued to speak about this, that they would be sued, so those people were harassed as they came out the door. They should not speak about this ever again. And so, in the context of that kind of harassment, I continued on with some of the, you know, couple of the families, and over the level of organizational divisions and some overt co-optation that occurred among the community leaders at that time, and it was just, you know, a very difficult, very painful period. So, at the time, then in '86 when we actually found evidence that all of these parties knew it, and in '84 to go back, when Vernon refused to take the data that the community had gathered, going door to door themselves, they had divided up, the women had said, "I'll take this part of the neighborhood," and they had done this very elaborate community health survey. State would not look at it. They gave it to the EPA, and the EPA now claims that they've lost it. It's been lost.

And so then we thought, well, why would be the motives? You know, what is... you know, again, why would the EPA allow? Why would the state allow this? Well, couple of significant things. And also on the Arsenal case, well, let me finish with the situation with the Attorney General. Two weeks ago, we called for Dr. Vernon to be, to resign, or in the event that he refused to resign, then we asked Governor Romer to fire him. We asked to meet with Governor Romer to show him the depth of the evidence that we have, have no less than 500 documents that all point to the charges that we have made gathered over a five year period. We hardly believe that we are acting frivolously and without adequate documentation, and certainly to take a five year period to bring these charges public. We don't think we're acting in haste. However, the governor has yet to meet with us. We have had no communications from his office when we pressed him on this publicly at a forum of the Rocky Flats group, which Philip taped in kind of a juicy little interchange, where I asked him publicly if he was planning to follow through on our request to investigate the state health department with the charges that we had, and he asked me to step away from the microphone and discontinue speaking.

We don't believe that's the case, because we have evidence of continuing criminal activity from the Water Board, and from the state, and from the EPA, and from the Martin Marietta, and so we don't think that that's a legitimate excuse, and on the other hand, if he did let the statute, if the statute did run, whose fault was that? Then, on the other hand, to say I need to have an executive order from the governor, we found very strange, because we don't think he had an executive order in '87 when we knew that they were proceeding. The lower level attorneys who had been assigned the case privately, told me that, you know, they rolled their eyes when asked about the Martin investigation, and they said, "Ask Woodard," kind of like that. So, you know, we suspect that Romer squished it at that time, or that Woodard decided, for his own political reasons, not to proceed, because none of the lower-level attorneys, none of the criminal investigators who were working with us on it indicated to us any, any problem with the statute, or that they were not seeing evidence of criminal activity. They were shocked, I mean, they were open, they were just floored by what we had, and so we think that's all very odd. So then Channel Seven with Woodard's letter in hand, then after our news conference, walked over to the governor's office and interviewed him. "Governor Romer, what do you think about, you know, the charges from the National Toxics Campaign that your state health department director is guilty of corruption and collusion in this scandal involving the Martin Marietta plant," and on camera the governor's response was the vein started bulging out of his collar, and he was very visibly upset, and he said, quote, "those are very radical charges. I don't treat them with much credibility." And then his whole... and then he stopped, and then his whole expression changed, and he kind of smiled. He said, "But I will, but I won't treat them that way. We will look into it." So, he, a week prior, had said publicly that he was calling for a criminal investigation. He said on camera the week following that he thought there were radical charges and not worth any credibility. We know that he's not looked at the charges and looked at the evidence, and he sent the thing, he threw the hot potato back over to Woodard, and that, and Channel Seven interviewed me live on the spot to respond to what Romer had said about us, and I said, "What's radical is that the state health department, for 30 years, would allow the poison of drinking water supply and not do anything about it. And we believe that if Romer and Woodard very quickly don't call for radical action to investigate this whole scandal that we believe that there's a need for a special prosecutor to be appointed in this, because it's clear that Romer and Woodard are in some ways complicit with allowing this not to be investigated." So that's where we are. Well, you know, I've not researched fully that all the different avenues that could be brought into that, but certainly we will, you know, go through other congressional avenues.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: [unintelligible] whole ball rolling with Rocky Flats [unintelligible]

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, see, this is what we think is really odd, that in the Rocky Flats allegations, they were alleging pollution of drinking water through the Walnut Creek and Woman Creek system, which would have polluted the drinking water. We have evidence of that in the Martin case. We have evidence of 30 years of that in the Martin case. And I did meet with the US Attorney's Office last summer, and they were quite shocked at what we had, and there was no prosecution forthcoming from that, and they also very clearly didn't follow through on even the most basic investigation that should have been done then, and so here the attorney, US attorney, is going after Rocky Flats, and so I have a lot of questions about what the motives are as to why they would be investigating Rocky Flats and not Martin Marietta.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: Mainly because they're going to, they're going to come and have findings that say everything is fine at Rocky Flats, and if they go to Martin Marietta, they won't? Something like that?

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, there are different theories, so I'll just lay them out, and you may have some of your own. One is that Bush is trying, with all of the political and public pressure about these Department of Energy facilities, that the Bush administration is now trying to appear to be credible on environmental regulation by taking the take... look tough attitude on this. They're also, I think, very worried about the fact that they are trying to get reauthorization for new monies to establish new facilities for plutonium production, because these are aged facilities. And that they want to build the case that these things can be done safely, so it's just been mismanagement of the DOE. Bush is going to come in and say we're going to clean these things up, build public perception that they can be done safely, so then that there's reauthorization for new monies to create new facilities, and they've, you know, come up with a big FBI investigation. This was theoretically started under the Reagan administration with a two-year time frame before they announced this investigation, but they didn't announce this investigation until after John Glenn, senator from Ohio, had introduced numbers of bills concerning the taking away the authority of the DOE to regulate its own facilities. And so there's all this pressure in Congress to strip away DOE's rights to investigate itself with congressional pressure, and there's also this question about how are we going to build new facilities, and the head of the DOE here, when he, the new guy that just came in, what's his name, DOE guy, I was up at a meeting, a meeting in Westminster with the area mayors, and the DOE guy admitted he said, "Well, you know, we have to operate Rocky Flat safely, so that either we can continue producing plutonium here or maybe we'll have to move our operations to a new location." So the question of stopping plutonium production is not in anyone's mind at the DOE, and that's that's my own personal theory. Now, there, you know, there are other theories that I've heard, and I don't give, I don't have credit, you know, I don't have evidence to any one of these theories, so it's up for grabs. But other people have suggested that US Attorney Mike Norton, having run against Wirth in that district up there, and now trying to position himself for other senate leanings, maybe trying to position himself on the Rocky Flats issue to position himself against Skaggs, who's taking some leadership role on that. That's one theory going around. But certainly, if you look at the weight of the evidence, there's Martin Marietta, is much better documented, and also unfortunately we believe the public health impact that's demonstrable from that is far greater than what we've seen from Rocky Plants, which I know is a shocking statement, but the cancer rates among children, the elevated rates are higher in southern Jefferson County than they are in northern Jefferson County, and something explains that difference. So we think there's a little political footsieing going on in some direction, but we're not quite sure how to understand it, and it's very odd to think that the FBI, from the Reagan administration to the Bush administration, can go from being the sort of organization that basically investigates people like all of us and is actually serving the public interest to break down the doors of Rocky Flats, and so I just really don't know. It's very curious. I mean, why did they not do this at Martin Marietta? You know, why a DOE facility? Why not...? And the other facility that they did the same type of action in, in New York, was also a nuclear facility. So we think there's some disparities in enforcement here, and we hope to get to the bottom of it, but certainly one of the things I'd like you to do tonight is write to Governor Romer. We have substantial evidence, not only on this case, but on the Rocky Mountain Arsenal situation that indicate that Vernon acted against the advice of his own staff people in the Rocky Mountain Arsenal case, which we can also talk about.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: I mean, you know, we can, we can do the gold plate model here, or the template, however long you want to go... But in the Arsenal case, evidence that when people were being overtly poisoned from the fumes coming off the Rocky Mountain Arsenal, the folks in the low-income trailer court next to the arsenal, the state allowed them to be gassed quite literally for seven months, fully knowing it the entire time, and failed to evacuate them, even against the advice of people in the Attorney General's office, as well as their own technical personnel in the epidemiology section, the state's head of epidemiology, as well as the state's toxicologist, and the site manager responsible for the arsenal, as well as individuals in the air quality division, all supported getting those people out of imminent danger from the poisoning, and Dr. Vernon stood up at a public meeting, and let's see... The Justice Department likes to quote from Vernon and Romer. Let me just give you a sampling of what our top leaders had to say about this. Governor Romer, December 21st, this is at the height of when people were getting the highest levels of aldrin and dieldrin, as well as nerve gas agents in the air in their yard, and their, you know, surrounding their homes. Governor Romer said, quote, "I have no evidence it requires evacuation now." 1988, this was this last Christmas. Governor Romer, December 30th, 1988. "The water is safe, the soil is safe, and the air is safe. I'm going to continue those tests, and I don't want anybody in danger." Now, we found evidence that the state health department had actually botched the air sampling that was done, and later had to correct its statements. When we do the calculations of what the aldrin and dieldrin levels were in the air surrounding these people's homes, the cancer risk that the EPA allows is acceptable is one cancer per million population. If you go above that, then they start suggesting that action, different actions are required to reduce the risk. We found that the calculations for aldrin with continuing exposure at the average of the levels that were found during this period in December would have put these people at the risk of developing cancer at one and 100, and even as high as one in 10, and those people were acutely ill. I got extremely ill myself, having gone out there and having been gassed by a cloud that came over when I was up there one day, my throat closed on the spot. I had laryngitis for three weeks, developed a large lump under my chin, and developed a blood disorder subsequent to that, that still hasn't resolved. The people who live there have got problems ranging from lumps on various parts of their body, from even chloracne type of symptoms, children with anemia, very severe anemia. One child that was born with underdeveloped arteries that was conceived during that period now is quite ill. And when I've gone up there to work with them,

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: [unintelligible] put them in a collar [unintelligible], cage and make them stay there.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Yeah, well, when I've been up there in the last few months, most of them are so despondent and ill that they can hardly function. A lot of them sleep virtually all day long. They're so ill. Yep. And we had a meeting with Governor Romer, excuse me, with Dr. Vernon in February, and the governor had ordered blood tests, had ordered medical testing of the residents with $25,000 that Shell ponied up for the governor's office, and he said, "Well, I'm going to see if these people have been, you know, I'm going to assure them that their health is fine." They, the, they had the Center for not... They had the Rocky Mountain Poison Control Center and the University of Colorado conduct the testing, but the physicians were told not to do testing for toxic chemicals in the blood, which are tests that can be done. So these people had routine blood tests done, you know, basic CBCs, and you know the basic parameters that won't tell you anything about whether or not you've been poisoned, but even those blood results came back abnormal for a number of the residents. Those were never publicized by the state. That's totally been swept under the rug. Now they want to take fat biopsies of the residents, and they're still allowing them to live there. Dr. Vernon... Now, what's at issue about that now? Is that this was all related to the Basin F cleanup, which is the word, which is a huge 93 acre liquid waste pond that had the accumulation of 40 years of army nerve gas production and Shell chemicals production of deadly pesticides that have since been banned by the EPA because of their acute toxicity. This site was even acknowledged by the Army to be the worst piece of property in the United States, if not the world, and it's right up in northeast Denver, right next to our brand new airport site. Yeah, I mean it's been pretty well publicly acknowledged. We have evidence of residents in that that are northwest of Rocky Mountain Arsenal, who, as of this day, continue to drink from municipal water well, not excuse me, not municipal... Private water wells that have nerve gas agents in them, and the state knows this, and the EPA knows this, and they have failed to close those wells, and also failed to provide alternative water to those people. The army and the EPA in 1986 came up, ponied up with $12 million to do charcoal filtration of the South Adams County Water District, which was poisoned by the contaminants coming off the Rocky Mountain Arsenal, South Adams County has a groundwater well, 100% groundwater well system that is supplied by the aquifer that is totally poisoned by the Rocky Mountain Arsenal. So we also have evidence that that water has been supplied to Commerce City residents for decades with knowledge that it was polluted. Now you know, you wonder why the people in Commerce City, you know, I've been working out there with seniors and others, you know, I've always, they're just kind of generally, I've always had a lot of people with learning disabilities in Commerce City, you know, kids that have various problems, and you know, it has always seemed like a community of people that are just not quite with it. And you know, while we might assume that's income or educational level or something else, I believe it's due to the poisoning, the, you know, consistent poisoning of these people over time. Knowing what I know now, those people are showing signs of solvent contamination with learning disabilities, and the kinds of gaps in some people, you know, stuttering speech, halting speech, not able to really fully articulate a sentence, and it's not because they're bright, but not bright, but it's evidence of solvent contamination. Now, after $12 million of treatment, we've done independent tests and found that that water still does not meet federal standards, and so these people are getting poisoned in the drinking water supply, they're also getting poisoned in the air. Now the Army came out today, saying it wants to incinerate all the liquids that they have pulled out of Basin F in the Denver metropolitan area. So, this is not only an issue... Onsite incineration of what is it, 4 million gallons of liquids that they have pulled out, some of the most acutely hazardous waste ever found anywhere in the world, and these are hundreds of compounds that have cooked for four decades in that site, mixed, commingled, created new compounds. They don't even have any idea what these things, what the toxicity of these things are now. Individually, many of them, there's no data about numbers of them individually, not to mention the complex mix of this stuff, they've currently got it stored. Oh, well, gee, so now they temporarily suck the stuff out in the process of sucking it out and drying the soils that were underneath of this, the gasses from the drying of the soils is what went into the Irondale community, just what was released from the process of taking the stuff out in a very crude technology that they used, you know, they project that this thing is going to cost $3 billion to clean up, and yet the technologies that they're using is very fourth grade in my opinion. And so they put several million gallons of it in these three tanks that are already beginning to leak, that were supposed to last for five years. They've started leaking now, within a few months of having put the liquids in, and they took the stuff out of the 93 acre pond and put the residual that wouldn't fit into the three tanks into yet another pond, just a, you know, few yards away, and that also has evidence, according to the state documents we've seen now, that is also leaking, so more stuff to leak, leach into the farms that are north of that site with wells that have already been poisoned and made in uninhabitable areas up there, and so the question now is, What to do with these millions of gallons? I know I'm really making you all happy here, but millions of gallons of acutely toxic waste that they've got stored in these huge, huge tanks, and I invite any of you to drive up there and just look at these, you know, these huge things that loom out on the horizon. There it looks like the moon, and then these huge tanks that stand up out of nowhere...

words: What the Basin F is, is a huge, like a vat. If you take all the liquid out of it, when the level, when the total level is low, the residual undissolved solids, which are precipitated on the bottom, remain.

words: So it's like pudding. Chocolate pudding.

words: ...high enough with add enough water to it, most of that sludge in the bottom will redissolve, and then you'll have, instead of 250 million liters, you might have a billion liters of solution with very little sediment on the bottom, but that sediment has got all sorts of junk in it. I've seen the analysis on it. I used to work there. I worked on Basin F once as a chemist, and they were at that time in '82 and '83, they were talking about solidifying it with concrete, and the only reason they funded with the nickels and dimes they had for the project I was on, which was defunded in '83 when the army unilaterally decided not to do anything with the arsenal whatsoever. When they were doing that, they were just giving us lip service, because they knew that encapsulating concrete was was silly.

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: So now, now everyone in town, I'm telling you, this is all out war, because the fact that the army would be proposing, well, there's another little war going on. The state attorney general's office is trying to get legal authority to oversee the cleanup of the arsenal. Now we have actually supported that, because we think, in general, as an institution, the state should have greater interest in the cleanup being protective of public health than what we've seen from the army and the EPA, and the army and the EPA, and these military sites act together. They do not act as adversarial parties, so you know basically what the army and the EPA say are together, because they're jointly represented by the Justice Department, and their positions are really very bad in our opinion, and so we do support the state having the authority, but with the caveat that we want someone else at the helm that is going to be actually working to protect public health and safety and not covering up these problems, so that's the kind of complexity going on at the moment, but it is Armageddon for the entire Denver metro... I mean, think of the contradiction in the big, you know, the big city that we're concerned about the brown cloud. It will become the black cloud. In fact, when we were driving up here, we looked over and there is a very discreet cloud hovering over the arsenal today, which we don't know what that means. Brown cloud, right, just a bubble over the arsenal, and we don't know what's going on there now, but the thought of having Basin F liquids incinerated in Denver, incineration is a very poor technology, it's probably the least protective technology in terms of regulation of what the EPA has, very poor monitoring requirements for incineration, and based upon what we saw with the Army's treatment of the Irondale residents. Oh in fact, the Army, in response to the residents' complaints, what was the Army's response to people saying "we're being gassed, we're waking up gasping at night, we can't breathe, our kids are sick, you know. My child gets up in the morning and throws up in the yard," this type of stuff? The army's response was to come out and bring Norelco air purifiers to each family that complained to put on their coffee tables. This was their solution.

speaker: Juc Speaker
words: Well, the incineration, getting back to that, what kind of technology are they proposing for incinerating these liquids?

speaker: Adrienne Anderson
words: Well, I don't know the specifics yet, but I'm going to a meeting on Thursday with the Attorney General's office, where we're going to be talking about all of this, but independent of what technology they're using for incineration, when we've studied this around the country, we certainly would be squawking very loudly that any type of incineration on site would put not only that Irondale area at immediate risk, but the entire metropolitan area, and there are millions of gallons of that stuff there. Worse, it's not - we don't believe it would just be a mechanism for getting rid of the onsite contaminants, but once the military has put in these types of facilities, they often then begin accepting hazardous waste from other military installations around the region. So, it will, we would predict, it would become a permanent incineration facility for all of the acutely toxic waste in the region. Worse, I learned today from Senator Gallagher, who represents North Denver, State Senator, that the EPA has announced plans to do on-site incineration at four other Superfund sites in North Denver, the Broderick Wood Product Superfund site, the - they're all kind of clustered up around Conoco, you know, up there by the interchange with Colorado Boulevard, and what's that? Yeah, yeah.

words: Vasquez.

words: Vasquez, that area there. There's four Superfund sites that are all in that vicinity, and the EPA is announcing plans to choose incineration as the preferred method of destruction.
